learning_objective: 🎯 Move from 2D to 3D! Learn how to shape, mold, and fire clay to create beautiful three-dimensional sculptures and pottery.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Paintings are 2D (flat, having height and width). Sculptures are 3D—they have height, width, and depth. You can walk around a sculpture and view it from all angles.

There are three basic ways to build with clay: 1) Pinching (shaping a ball of clay with your thumb), 2) Coiling (rolling clay into snake-like ropes and stacking them), and 3) Slabbing (rolling clay into flat sheets).
Just like the human body needs a skeleton to stand up, tall or complex sculptures need an 'armature'. It is an internal frame, usually made of wire, that supports the soft clay.
Terracotta (meaning 'baked earth') is a type of brownish-red clay. Once shaped, it is dried and baked at very high temperatures in an oven called a 'Kiln' to make it hard and permanent.
A sculpture 'in-the-round' stands alone and can be seen from all sides. A 'relief' sculpture is carved into a flat wall or panel, projecting outwards like a 3D painting.

fun_activity.title: 🐍 The Coil Pot
fun_activity.instructions: Take some playdough or natural clay. Roll it out into long, thin 'snakes'. Roll the first snake into a flat spiral (this is the base). Now, stack the remaining snakes on top of the outer edge of the base, building up the walls to make a pot!

exam_tips: 📌 Clearly explain the difference between a 2D painting and a 3D sculpture.
📌 Know the three basic clay hand-building techniques: Pinch, Coil, and Slab.
📌 Remember that unbaked clay will melt in water, but once fired in a 'Kiln', it becomes permanent Terracotta/Ceramic.
quick_recap: ⭐ An armature provides essential structural support for clay figures so they don't collapse.
⭐ Relief sculptures are often found on the walls of ancient Indian temples.
⭐ Keeping clay wet while working is important, as it cracks and breaks if it dries out too fast.
